The death of the American university system.
I doubt that will happen in 10 years.

It might be closer than you think. In 1965, universities had a great alumni base. They went to college for a the price of a nice suit each year, watched some great football, had a nice time. These people gave lots of money later. Sure, some stopped giving money when filthy hippies, co-eds, and coloreds showed up. But that new wave started basing memories in rock music, weed, and a copious supply of fresh ass. That inspired a new wave of giving alumni. College became a standardized experience. The 80s had yuppies who had money to give and often had class aspirations that made the most successful want to make a show of "giving back".

What's changed? Since the 90s, most alumni haven't had great jobs. Our memories are culled from a four year shitshow of social programming that inspires SJWs. The universities were awash in money because corporations had figured out that they could fob R&D off on university partnerships. The synergy was more palatable than stealing from interns. Post-Docs are used to giving away their work. So, now there's about a solid generation of people who were saddled with more than a year's wages worth of debt. The universities have grown their endowments, but they have costs -- and rapidly declining social capital. How many people with student loans plan on returning anything to the entity that enabled their debt? Ex-hippies are still the biggest donors to universities.

Rather than shore up their image, universities are now hoping to attract Chinese students. There's a fucking brilliant plan. These "foreign capital" projects lower their academic standards. Perhaps more importantly, it does not create a loyal alumni base. Universities have almost systematically sold out their long-term backers in search of growth and new audiences. I'd say they're an economic crisis away from disappearing now. Given a repeat of 2008, endowments will look like a juicy plum for officials hoping to balance their debt... for another election cycle. (Harvard revised its tuition plan when MA cast an eye toward it.)
